strengths: Answers a clear open question: establishes the first fine-grained gap-dependent regret upper bound of the form sum over suboptimal triples of 1/Delta_h(s,a) plus |Zopt|/Delta_min for a model-free (UCB-based) algorithm, matching the model-based state of the art in structure; the paper convincingly argues why model-based techniques (surplus analysis with an empirical kernel) do not transfer directly to model-free methods, which justifies the need for a new framework.

The proposed analytical framework (per-state-action weighting, recursive propagation of weighted estimation errors across steps, and separate Cauchy–Schwarz treatment of optimal vs. suboptimal pairs) is well motivated and appears genuinely novel; the inductive argument in Lemma 3.4/E.5 is technically involved and the main theorems are supported by detailed, self-contained proofs in the appendix.

The identification of two concrete flaws in the AMB algorithm (Xu et al., 2021) — truncation at H and 0 breaking the equality needed for optimism/pessimism, and centering of bootstrap estimators around expectations rather than conditional expectations violating the martingale difference condition — is carefully argued in Section G.1, and the proposed Refined AMB restores rigor via a nontrivial induction establishing unbiasedness of the multi-step bootstrapping decomposition (Theorem G.1).

Demonstrates generality of the framework by applying it to a second algorithm (ULCB-Hoeffding) achieving the same fine-grained bound, and provides both worst-case and gap-dependent guarantees; the theoretical results are complemented by reproducible code and empirical comparisons consistent with the logarithmic-regret theory.

Positioning against prior work (Yang et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2025b; Simchowitz & Jamieson, 2019; Chen et al., 2025) is thorough, including an honest technical comparison (Appendix C) explaining why the model-based proof strategies fail in the model-free setting, and a discussion of lower-bound tightness of the |Zopt|/Delta_min term.
weaknesses: The polynomial dependence on H is loose: the gap-dependent terms scale as H^5/Delta_h(s,a), which is H^3 worse than the model-based state of the art (H^2/Delta_h(s,a) in Chen et al., 2025), and the 'matching the lower bound' claim holds only up to polynomial factors in H. Given that reducing H-dependence was precisely the motivation for improvements over Yang et al. (2021) (H^6), the significance of the improvement over prior model-free results should be assessed more carefully.

The claim that AMB (a published COLT 2021 paper) is flawed is a strong assertion; while the arguments in Sections 4 and G.1 are plausible, a reviewer cannot fully verify them without reconstructing Xu et al.'s analysis. If correct, this is valuable; however, the paper should provide a sharper, verifiable counterexample or a more precise localization of the error to strengthen the case.

Experimental evaluation is weak: only tiny synthetic tabular MDPs (S <= 15, A <= 10, H <= 10) with uniformly random rewards and transitions, a single MDP instance per setting, and 10 runs. The experiments do not probe MDPs where the fine-grained gap structure matters (e.g., varying Delta_min, number of optimal actions), and notably UCB-Hoeffding performs best, which somewhat undercuts the practical value of the more complex ULCB/Refined AMB variants.

The main contribution for UCB-based algorithms is a new analysis of an existing algorithm (UCB-Hoeffding) rather than a new algorithm or a fundamentally tighter result; ULCB-Hoeffding is largely a simplification of AMB with the bootstrapping removed, so the incremental novelty relative to Zhang et al. (2025a, 2025b) style reference-advantage analyses should be clarified.

The fine-grained term involving (sum_t sqrt|Zopt,t|)^2 / Delta_min,h is somewhat awkward and the relationship to the cleaner |Zopt|/Delta_min form only holds in restricted regimes; a comparison table consolidating all gap-dependent bounds (model-free and model-based) would substantially improve readability and positioning.

Several proofs rely on large hidden constants (e.g., c1 = 20736, c2 = 82944) and lengthy AM-GM/absorption steps; while not incorrect as far as can be checked, the constants make the results far from tight and hard to interpret.

strengths: Addresses a clearly stated open question: whether fine-grained, instance-dependent (per-gap) regret bounds are achievable for model-free RL, where prior model-free results only gave coarse SA/Δ_min-type bounds while model-based works (Simchowitz & Jamieson 2019; Dann et al. 2021; Chen et al. 2025) achieved fine-grained bounds.

Establishes the first fine-grained gap-dependent regret bound for a UCB-based model-free algorithm (UCB-Hoeffding) via a genuinely new analytical framework that treats optimal and suboptimal state-action pairs separately, exploiting the fact that suboptimal pairs are visited only Õ(log T) times. The recursive weight machinery (Lemmas 3.2-3.4) appears technically nontrivial and is reusable, as demonstrated by its application to ULCB-Hoeffding.

Careful and well-documented identification of two concrete flaws in AMB (Xu et al., 2021): (i) the truncations at H and 0 in the Q-updates break the equality needed for their Equation (A.5), and (ii) the concentration analysis centers estimators on expectations rather than conditional expectations, violating the martingale-difference condition for Azuma-Hoeffding. The detailed diagnosis in Section G.1 is a valuable service to the community.

The proposed refinements are principled: ULCB-Hoeffding simplifies AMB by dropping multi-step bootstrapping while retaining the same fine-grained bound, and Refined AMB rigorously re-establishes optimism/pessimism (Theorem G.1) with an unbiasedness proof for the bootstrapping estimators (Section G.3).

The tightness discussion is more careful than typical: the result is compared against the Simchowitz & Jamieson lower bound and the |Zmul|/Δ_min lower bound of Xu et al., and Appendix C.2 gives a substantive technical comparison explaining why model-based surplus arguments do not transfer to model-free methods.
Worst-case guarantees are preserved (Theorem 4.1 matches the √T-type bound), and code is provided with reproducibility statements.
weaknesses: The gap-dependent terms carry heavy polynomial factors in H (H^5 per-gap term, H^5|Zopt|/Δ_min in the simplified form), which are substantially worse than the model-based state of the art (Chen et al., 2025: H^2 per-gap and H^2|Zopt|/Δ_min). This weakens the practical significance of the 'fine-grained' improvement: the gains relative to Yang et al. (2021) come mainly from replacing SA with per-gap sums, while a large constant-factor (in H) looseness remains.

The claimed motivation for Refined AMB is that multi-step bootstrapping improves dependence on 1/Δ_min, yet the final bound (Equation 11) retains a |Zmul|/Δ_min term with the same H^5 scaling, and its second term is weaker than the UCB-based bound's |Zopt|/Δ_min. The concrete advantage of the non-UCB refinement over ULCB-Hoeffding is not clearly demonstrated, theoretically or empirically.

The empirical evaluation is very limited: only small synthetic tabular MDPs (H ≤ 10, S ≤ 15), a single randomly generated MDP instance, only 10 trajectories, and no comparison against other gap-dependent model-free algorithms with known bounds (e.g., UCB-Advantage or Q-EarlySettled-Advantage analyzed by Zheng et al., 2025b). The observation that plain UCB-Hoeffding performs best overall somewhat undercuts the practical value of the more complex refinements.

The contribution is primarily analytical: the algorithms are either existing (UCB-Hoeffding) or close variants of prior work (AMB), so the novelty rests on the proof techniques. The framework's applicability beyond UCB-Hoeffding/ULCB-Hoeffding is asserted (e.g., UCB-Bernstein, UCB-Advantage) but not carried out.

Several statements about improvements are stated in idealized regimes (e.g., a single suboptimal triple, |Zopt| independent of A), and the extent to which the bound dominates Yang et al. (2021) in practically relevant regimes could be debated given the differing polynomial factors.

Correctness of ~45 pages of proofs is hard to fully verify in review; while the structure looks sound, some steps (e.g., the tight constants c1=20736, c2=82944 and the weight-bound arguments in Lemma D.4) rely on delicate bookkeeping that would benefit from independent verification.

strengths: Addresses a clearly stated and genuinely open question: whether fine-grained gap-dependent regret bounds with individual suboptimality gaps Δh(s,a) can be established for model-free (tabular) RL, where only coarse-grained SA/Δmin bounds existed for UCB-based algorithms.

Establishes the first fine-grained gap-dependent regret bound for the canonical UCB-Hoeffding algorithm (Jin et al., 2018), and the bound's dependence on |Zopt|/Δmin provably matches known lower bounds (Simchowitz & Jamieson 2019; Xu et al. 2021) up to polynomial factors in H, supporting the tightness of the result.

Provides a valuable service to the community by carefully identifying two concrete technical flaws in the analysis of AMB (Xu et al., 2021, COLT): improper truncation of Q-estimates that breaks a key recursive identity, and violation of the martingale-difference condition in the concentration argument. Section G.1 gives a detailed and convincing diagnosis.

The proposed analytical framework (per-state-action weighted estimation error recursion, Lemmas 3.2–3.4) is a genuine technical contribution that also applies to a second algorithm (ULCB-Hoeffding), demonstrating generality.
Full and detailed proofs are provided in the appendix (Sections D–G), including careful technical lemmas; the writing is clear and the proof sketch in the main text is readable.
Includes experiments on four scales with code provided, showing empirical improvements of the proposed refinements over original AMB, and regret curves consistent with the logarithmic-growth theory.
Reproducibility statement and code availability are adequate; experiments are lightweight (12 hours on a desktop).
weaknesses: The overall significance is moderate: the result is essentially closing a gap left open between model-based fine-grained bounds (Simchowitz & Jamieson 2019; Dann et al. 2021; Chen et al. 2025) and model-free methods, but with substantially worse polynomial H-dependence (H^5 log(SAT)/Δh(s,a) vs. H^2/Δh(s,a) for model-based works), so the final bound is far from the model-based state of the art.

The contribution is incremental relative to prior art: it builds directly on the visitation-pattern observation of Zhang et al. (2025a) (Lemma 4.1), the gap-dependent analysis of Yang et al. (2021) and Zheng et al. (2025b), and the structure of AMB; the Refined AMB bound (Equation 11) is largely recovered by 'adapting the remaining arguments of Xu et al. (2021)', which slightly weakens the claim of a self-contained rigorous correction.

There is a mild tension in the narrative: if the AMB analysis of Xu et al. (2021) is invalid, then reusing its 'remaining arguments' for Refined AMB requires justification that is only sketched (Section G.4), and the H^5 factor in Equation (11) is worse than the claimed AMB bound style.

Experiments are limited to small synthetic tabular MDPs with uniformly random rewards/transitions, a single MDP instance per scale, 10 trajectories, and no real-world tasks or strong baseline comparisons beyond the four algorithms studied; notably UCB-Hoeffding (an existing algorithm) performs best, which somewhat undercuts the practical motivation for the proposed refinements.

The main theorem is stated in expectation only; a high-probability version of the fine-grained bound for UCB-Hoeffding is not provided, which would be the more standard formulation in this literature.

Large hidden constants (e.g., c1 = 20736, c2 = 82944) and loose inequality chains mean the bounds, while asymptotically meaningful, may be very loose in practice; the empirical section does not attempt to validate the practical tightness of the theoretical constants.

Impact is confined to the narrow sub-area of tabular, model-free RL theory; the framework's claimed extensibility to stronger model-free algorithms (UCB-Advantage, Q-EarlySettled-Advantage, Bernstein variants) is left as future work.
